expectedText:
DEPLOYED PARENT CUSTODY AND VISITATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · John Smith

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet explains California Family Code section 3047, the statute that addresses child custody and visitation orders when a parent or party is activated to military duty, mobilized, or deployed. It covers what the statute says about: modification of existing orders due to a party's military absence, the temporary and reversible nature of any resulting order change, visitation rights the court may extend to a stepparent, grandparent, or other family member during a deploying party's absence, expedited-hearing and remote-participation options before a party departs, and the statute's effect on continuing court jurisdiction under the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act (UCCJEA) during deployment. It does NOT calculate or propose a specific custody or visitation schedule for Alex Doe, does not tell Jane Doe or John Smith whether to file a motion or what outcome to request, and does not substitute for advice from a licensed attorney about a particular family's situation. This sheet is distinct from a move-away/relocation custody information sheet, which addresses a parent's voluntary decision to relocate with a child for reasons unrelated to military orders, and from an emergency custody order information sheet, which addresses ex parte emergency relief generally. This sheet is not a substitute for reading the full text of Family Code section 3047 or for consulting the court or a licensed attorney about a specific case.

MILITARY ABSENCE ALONE IS NOT GROUNDS FOR MODIFICATION
Under California Family Code section 3047(a), a party's absence, relocation, or failure to comply with an existing custody or visitation order does not, by itself, justify modifying that order when the reason is the party's activation to military duty or temporary duty, mobilization in support of a combat or other military operation, or military deployment out of state.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A party’s absence, relocation, or failure to comply with custody and visitation orders shall not, by itself, be sufficient to justify a modification of a custody or visitation order if the reason for the absence, relocation, or failure to comply is the party’s activation to military duty or temporary duty, mobilization in support of combat or other military operation, or military deployment out of state."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(a), Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3047.)
  Known gap: The statute states this rule as a limit on using military absence alone as grounds for modification; it does not exempt a party from every possible ground for modification, and it does not define how a court weighs this factor against other best-interest considerations in a contested proceeding. No case law analysis was performed for this clause (see the CourtListener research-limitation note in the document-level disclosure); this clause is based on statutory text only.

MODIFICATIONS DURING DEPLOYMENT ARE TEMPORARY, WITH A PRESUMPTION OF REVERSION
Under California Family Code section 3047(b)(1)-(2), when a party with sole or joint physical custody or visitation receives temporary duty, deployment, or mobilization orders that require moving a substantial distance or that otherwise materially affect the party's ability to exercise custody or visitation, any resulting modification of the existing custody order is deemed a temporary order made without prejudice. When that temporary order is reviewed upon the party's return, there is a presumption that the custody order will revert to what was in place before the modification, unless the court determines reversion is not in the child's best interest. The statute also provides that the court is not to order a child custody evaluation under Family Code section 3111 or Evidence Code section 730 as part of that return review, unless the party opposing reversion makes a prima facie showing that reversion is not in the child's best interest.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If a party with sole or joint physical custody or visitation receives temporary duty, deployment, or mobilization orders from the military that require the party to move a substantial distance from the party’s residence or otherwise has a material effect on the ability of the party to exercise custody or visitation rights, any necessary modification of the existing custody order shall be deemed a temporary custody order made without prejudice, which shall be subject to review and reconsideration upon the return of the party from military deployment, mobilization, or temporary duty."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(b)(1), Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3047.)
  "If the temporary order is reviewed upon return of the party from military deployment, mobilization, or temporary duty, there shall be a presumption that the custody order shall revert to the order that was in place before the modification, unless the court determines that it is not in the best interest of the child. The court shall not, as part of its review of the temporary order upon the return of the deploying party, order a child custody evaluation under Section 3111 of this code or Section 730 of the Evidence Code, unless the party opposing reversion of the order makes a prima facie showing that reversion is not in the best interest of the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(b)(2), Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(b)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3047.)
  Known gap: The statute does not define 'substantial distance' or specify how a court determines whether an effect on custody or visitation ability is 'material'; those determinations are left to case-by-case application. No case law analysis was performed for this clause (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time — see document-level disclosure); this clause is based on statutory text only.

VISITATION FOR A STEPPARENT, GRANDPARENT, OR OTHER FAMILY MEMBER DURING DEPLOYMENT
Under California Family Code section 3047(b)(3), when a court makes a temporary custody order because of a party's military duty, deployment, or mobilization, the court is to consider appropriate orders to help the relocating party maintain frequent and continuing contact with the child. On a motion by the relocating party, the court may grant reasonable visitation rights to a stepparent, grandparent, or other family member if the court finds a preexisting bonded relationship between that family member and the child such that visitation is in the child's best interest, finds the visitation will facilitate the child's contact with the relocating party, and balances the child's interest in that visitation against the parents' right to exercise parental authority. The statute states that this provision does not increase the family member's independent authority to seek visitation, and that visitation granted to a nonparent under this provision does not affect the calculation of child support.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Upon a motion by the relocating party, the court may grant reasonable visitation rights to a stepparent, grandparent, or other family member if the court does all of the following:(i) Finds that there is a preexisting relationship between the family member and the child that has engendered a bond such that visitation is in the best interest of the child.(ii) Finds that the visitation will facilitate the child’s contact with the relocating party.(iii) Balances the interest of the child in having visitation with the family member against the right of the parents to exercise parental authority."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(b)(3), Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(b)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3047.)
  "This paragraph does not increase the authority of the persons described in subparagraph (B) to seek visitation orders independently.(D) The granting of visitation rights to a nonparent pursuant to subparagraph (B) shall not impact the calculation of child support."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(b)(3)(C)-(D), Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(b)(3)(C)-(D) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3047.)
  Known gap: This family-member visitation right arises only on a motion by the relocating (deploying) party in this specific temporary-order context under section 3047(b)(3); the statute expressly states it does not create an independent right for a stepparent, grandparent, or other family member to seek visitation on their own. It does not describe how courts apply the three required findings in practice. No case law analysis was performed for this clause (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time — see document-level disclosure); this clause is based on statutory text only.

EXPEDITED HEARINGS AND REMOTE PARTICIPATION BEFORE DEPLOYMENT
Under California Family Code section 3047(c), when a party's deployment, mobilization, or temporary duty will materially affect that party's ability, or anticipated ability, to appear in person at a regularly scheduled hearing, the court is to do either of two things on the party's motion: hold an expedited hearing to determine custody and visitation issues before the party departs, or allow the party to present testimony and evidence and participate in court-ordered child custody mediation by electronic means — including telephone, video teleconferencing, or the internet — to the extent that technology is reasonably available to the court and protects the due process rights of all parties.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If a party’s deployment, mobilization, or temporary duty will have a material effect on the party’s ability, or anticipated ability, to appear in person at a regularly scheduled hearing, the court shall do either of the following:(1) Upon motion of the party, hold an expedited hearing to determine custody and visitation issues prior to the departure of the party.(2) Upon motion of the party, allow the party to present testimony and evidence and participate in court-ordered child custody mediation by electronic means, including, but not limited to, telephone, video teleconferencing, or the internet, to the extent that this technology is reasonably available to the court and protects the due process rights of all parties."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(c), Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3047.)
  Known gap: The statute conditions electronic participation on the technology being 'reasonably available to the court,' a standard that is not further defined and may vary by county and courtroom. No case law analysis was performed for this clause (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time — see document-level disclosure); this clause is based on statutory text only.

EFFECT ON CONTINUING COURT JURISDICTION UNDER THE UCCJEA
Family Code section 3047(d) states that a relocation by a nondeploying parent during the period of a deployed parent's absence, while a temporary modification order for a parenting plan is in effect, does not by itself terminate the court's exclusive and continuing jurisdiction. Section 3047(e) states that when a California court has issued a custody or visitation order, a child's absence from the state during a parent's deployment is considered a 'temporary absence' for purposes of the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act (Family Code section 3400 et seq.), and the court retains exclusive continuing jurisdiction under Family Code section 3422. Section 3047(f) states that a parent's deployment cannot be used as a basis to assert inconvenient forum under Family Code section 3427.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A relocation by a nondeploying parent during a period of a deployed parent’s absence while a temporary modification order for a parenting plan is in effect shall not, by itself, terminate the exclusive and continuing jurisdiction of the court for purposes of later determining custody or parenting time under this chapter."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(d), Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3047.)
  "When a court of this state has issued a custody or visitation order, the absence of a child from this state during the deployment of a parent shall be considered a “temporary absence” for purposes of the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act (Part 3 (commencing with Section 3400)), and the court shall retain exclusive continuing jurisdiction under Section 3422.(f) The deployment of a parent shall not be used as a basis to assert inconvenience of the forum under Section 3427."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(e)-(f), Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(e)-(f) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3047.)
  Known gap: These provisions describe how deployment interacts with the UCCJEA's jurisdiction and inconvenient-forum rules in general terms; they do not resolve jurisdiction disputes involving courts of other states or countries, which depend on the full text of Family Code sections 3400–3465 and that jurisdiction's own law. No case law analysis was performed for this clause (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time — see document-level disclosure); this clause is based on statutory text only.

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS: DEPLOYMENT, MOBILIZATION, AND TEMPORARY DUTY
Family Code section 3047(g) defines three terms used throughout the statute. 'Deployment' means the temporary transfer of a member of the Armed Forces in active-duty status in support of combat or some other military operation. 'Mobilization' means the transfer of a member of the National Guard or Military Reserve to extended active-duty status, but does not include National Guard or Military Reserve annual training. 'Temporary duty' means the transfer of a servicemember from one military base to a different location, usually another base, for a limited period of time to accomplish training or to assist in the performance of a noncombat mission.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Deployment” means the temporary transfer of a member of the Armed Forces in active-duty status in support of combat or some other military operation.(2) “Mobilization” means the transfer of a member of the National Guard or Military Reserve to extended active-duty status, but does not include National Guard or Military Reserve annual training.(3) “Temporary duty” means the transfer of a servicemember from one military base to a different location, usually another base, for a limited period of time to accomplish training or to assist in the performance of a noncombat mission."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(g), Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(g) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3047.)
  Known gap: These definitions apply only 'for purposes of this section' (Family Code section 3047) and may not carry the same meaning in other statutes or in federal military law such as the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act. National Guard or Military Reserve annual training is expressly excluded from 'mobilization.' No case law analysis was performed for this clause (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time — see document-level disclosure); this clause is based on statutory text only.

STATEMENT OF LEGISLATIVE INTENT
Family Code section 3047(h) states that it is the intent of the Legislature that section 3047 provide a fair, efficient, and expeditious process to resolve child custody and visitation issues when a party receives temporary duty, deployment, or mobilization orders, and at the time the party returns and moves to revert to the prior custody order. The statute states the Legislature's intent that family courts, to the extent feasible within existing resources and court practices, prioritize the calendaring of these cases, avoid unnecessary delay or continuances, and ensure that parties who serve in the military are not penalized for their service by delay in appropriate access to their children.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "It is the intent of the Legislature that this section provide a fair, efficient, and expeditious process to resolve child custody and visitation issues when a party receives temporary duty, deployment, or mobilization orders from the military, as well as at the time that the party returns from service and files a motion to revert back to the custody order in place before the deployment. The Legislature intends that family courts shall, to the extent feasible within existing resources and court practices, prioritize the calendaring of these cases, avoid unnecessary delay or continuances, and ensure that parties who serve in the military are not penalized for their service by a delay in appropriate access to their children."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(h), Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(h) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3047.)
  Known gap: A legislative-intent statement expresses purpose and expectation; it directs courts on calendaring priorities 'to the extent feasible within existing resources and court practices' but does not itself create an enforceable deadline or a specific remedy if a court does not prioritize a case. No case law analysis was performed for this clause (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time — see document-level disclosure); this clause is based on statutory text only.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This information sheet was prepared for Jane Doe and/or John Smith regarding the child or children known as Alex Doe, for filing or reference in San Diego County, in connection with proceedings before Superior Court of California, County of San Diego. It reflects the statutory text of Family Code section 3047 as of the date checked above and is provided for informational purposes only. It is not legal advice, does not recommend any particular custody or visitation arrangement, and does not state what Jane Doe or John Smith should do. By signing below, the person completing this sheet acknowledges reading it and understands that it summarizes California statutory law without addressing the facts of any specific case.
